papers.title: Effects of Sacred Dances versus Conventional Physical Training on Functional Capacity and Quality of Life in Women with Heart Failure: Protocol for a Randomized Active-Controlled Crossover Non-Inferiority Trial (RED-WHF)
papers.abstract: This protocol describes the RED-WHF trial, a randomized, active-controlled, two-period crossover clinical trial designed to evaluate whether Sacred Dances (SD)--as a mind-body intervention--are non-inferior to conventional physical training (PT) regarding functional capacity and quality of life in women with heart failure (HF). Sedentary behavior and emotional stress significantly worsen HF prognosis, yet conventional exercise programs face barriers in patient adherence and variable motivation. Sacred Dances, a form of low-to-moderate-intensity moving meditation, may enhance physical fitness while promoting emotional well-being and spiritual connection (flourishing). We will recruit 30 sedentary women aged 18 to 70 with stable HF (NYHA class I-III) and a documented left ventricular ejection fraction. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to one of two treatment sequences: SD followed by PT, or vice versa. Each 12-week intervention phase consists of two weekly sessions, lasting 90 minutes for SD (with 60 minutes of active dancing to allow choreography instruction) and 60 minutes for PT, separated by a 3-week washout period. Primary outcomes are functional capacity (6-minute walk test [6MWT]) and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L Index and VAS). Secondary outcomes include adherence rates, spiritual attitudes (ARES scale), symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress (DASS-21), and perceived subjective impact (EUPI-12). Statistical planning incorporates linear mixed models (LMM) with treatment, period, and sequence fixed effects, and an intention-to-treat approach with multiple imputation for missing data. To establish non-inferiority, a 30-meter margin for the 6MWT difference will be applied. The study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (CEP/EBMSP opinion 7.443.180, CAAE: 86133125.0.0000.5544) and prospectively registered in the Brazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (ReBEC ID: RBR-85tkdz5).

papers.title: Expert-level localization of fine-grained cardiac structures across the transthoracic echocardiogram
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence models for echocardiography interpret studies without identifying the structures that support their outputs. We show that this spatial grounding does not emerge from the pretraining of current vision-language models. General-purpose and medical vision-language models and an open-vocabulary detector recalled 3% or fewer of cardiac structures and scored below a box that never sees the image. EchoLens, a detector trained on 5,912 expert-annotated structures and 4,219 Doppler signals from 136 patients, recalled 87% and localized structures as reliably as a blinded expert reader (box centre within the reference in 95.7% and 95.3% of cases). It covers 21 structures across 11 transthoracic views and 11 spectral Doppler signal types. In external data, two physicians judged 81-92% of its detections correct across all 11 views, and it identified the Doppler signal type in 83% of frames. EchoLens provides the spatial layer that grounded echocardiographic interpretation requires.

papers.title: Cytokine Signatures of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Myocarditis and the Modifying Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis: A Machine-Learning and Multi-Omics Study
papers.abstract: Background Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis affects up to 2% of patients on ICI and has up to a 50% mortality. Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is a risk factor for ICI myocarditis. Objectives: To leverage a multi-omics approach to evaluate cytokines associated with ICI myocarditis, immunosuppression resistance, CHIP in ICI myocarditis and implicated pathways and cell type contributions. Methods 236 cardio-oncology patients were enrolled, including 88 who were on ICI. Cytokine profiling from patients on ICI were sampled and analyzed using machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence. Single-cell multi-omics of peripheral blood from Yale (n=19), Stanford (n=25), and MGH (n=63) evaluated cell-type contributions of cytokines and implicated pathways. Validation of Yale proteomic analyses was done using the Stanford CYTOF dataset. Results Top features associated with ICI myocarditis included IL13, CXCL10, PDGFA, CCL13, CCL17 and KITlg. Top KEGG pathways associated with ICI myocarditis and immunosuppression resistant ICI myocarditis included JAK STAT signaling, IL17 signaling and lipid/atherosclerosis pathways. At the single-cell level, the consensus signals distinguishing myocarditis from non-myocarditis across cohorts was predominantly driven by module-level JAK STAT, T cell, and Toll like receptor activation. Similar transcription gene programs were activated in CHIP carriers including modules implicated in the pro-inflammatory immune response, such as NF kappa B, IL17, MAPK, and TNF pathways within CHIP cells spanning lymphoid (cytotoxic CD8+ NKT, and natural killer cells) and myeloid lineages. Conclusions Across cohorts, JAK STAT signaling emerges as a convergent and potentially actionable axis in ICI myocarditis that is further amplified in CHIP carriers, supporting cytokine-guided risk stratification and JAK STAT directed immunosuppression as testable strategies.

papers.title: Nationwide Functional Profiling Enables Clinical Reclassification of KCNH2 Variants in the French LQT2 Population
papers.abstract: Background: The increasing use of genetic testing has identified thousands of KCNH2 variants associated with long QT syndrome type 2 (LQT2), yet most remain variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Translating functional abnormalities into clinically actionable evidence remains a major challenge. We established a nationwide functional genomics strategy to systematically characterize KCNH2 variants identified in the French LQT2 population and improve their clinical interpretation. Methods: We characterized 303 KCNH2 variants, including 201 VUS, using standardized high-throughput automated patch-clamp electrophysiology and complementary membrane trafficking assays. Nine electrophysiological parameters were integrated using MeTAL to predict variant-specific repolarization phenotypes under homozygous and heterozygous conditions. Modeled QTc values were compared with patient electrocardiographic data and variant-specific penetrance estimates. Functional evidence was calibrated against established benign and pathogenic variants using ClinGen-recommended categorical OddsPath and continuous likelihood-ratio approaches. Results: Multidimensional functional profiling revealed abnormalities not captured by current amplitude alone, identifying additional variants with clinically relevant repolarization defects. Among variants assessed under heterozygous conditions, MeTAL predictions showed 82.9% concordance with patient QTc phenotypes for ACMG class 5 variants, with apparent discordances partly consistent with incomplete penetrance. Continuous likelihood-ratio calibration demonstrated strong discrimination between established benign and pathogenic variants (AUC=0.936) and provided graded functional evidence for 76.1% of VUS. Integration of calibrated functional evidence into the ACMG/AMP framework enabled reclassification of 64 of 201 VUS (31.8%), including 7 as pathogenic, 46 as likely pathogenic, and 11 as likely benign. Conclusions: This nationwide study establishes a scalable framework integrating high-throughput electrophysiology, computational modeling, and clinical phenotyping to translate complex KCNH2 channel dysfunction into clinically interpretable evidence. The resulting reclassification of nearly one-third of VUS, together with the open-access HAMMER database, provides a resource to improve molecular diagnosis and risk assessment in LQT2.

papers.title: Beat-to-beat blood pressure variability and Alzheimers disease pathophysiology
papers.abstract: Introduction: Elevated blood pressure variability (BPV) is predictive of Alzheimers disease neuropathologic change observed with AD biomarkers. However, prior studies have largely focused on visit-to-visit BPV, which may be influenced by antihypertensive medication adherence and other external factors. Few studies have investigated beat-to-beat BPV, a reliable and direct measure of cardiovascular and autonomic function relevant to AD. Methods: Independently living older adults (N=132) were recruited from the community. Participants underwent continuous blood pressure monitoring and venipuncture. Plasma p-Tau217, p-Tau181, GFAP, NfL, and amyloid-{beta}42/40 ratio were assessed. Linear regression examined the relationship between beat-to-beat systolic BPV and plasma AD biomarkers with and without adjustment for age, sex, systolic blood pressure, and apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) carrier status. Results: Elevated beat-to-beat BPV was associated with elevated plasma p-Tau217 ({beta}=0.32, p=0.008), plasma p-Tau181 ({beta}=0.22, p=0.05), and plasma GFAP ({beta}=0.41, p=0.00001). Elevated BPV was not associated with plasma amyloid-{beta}42/40 ratio or plasma NfL. Discussion: Increased beat-to-beat BPV is associated with increased Core 1 T1 biomarkers of phosphorylated and secreted AD tau in blood plasma (i.e., pTau217, pTau181), but not with amyloid-{beta}42/40 ratio, a biomarker more exclusively indexing cerebral amyloid retention alone. Elevated BPV was also associated with higher plasma GFAP, a marker of astrocyte reactivity. These findings are consistent with prior studies relating visit-to-visit BPV to AD biomarkers, suggesting that intrinsic cardiovascular and/or autonomic factors underlie links between BPV and AD.

papers.title: Electromechanical Drivers of Diastolic Dysfunction During Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Progression
papers.abstract: Aims: Diastolic dysfunction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy reflects changes in sarcomeric function, electrophysiology, ventricular structure, and myocardial mechanics. Their effects on filling remain difficult to determine clinically. We sought to dissect these effects in MYH7-related non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy progression. Methods and results: We developed a human biventricular electromechanical model linking electrophysiology and calcium handling to contraction, ventricular mechanics, haemodynamics, electrocardiography, and myocardial strain. Stage I represented MYH7 sarcomeric dysfunction before hypertrophy; Stage II added septal hypertrophy; Stage III added increased myocardial stiffness. Secondary ionic remodelling was examined at each stage and severity. Sarcomeric dysfunction alone generated a low-volume hypercontractile phenotype before overt hypertrophy. Septal hypertrophy further constrained chamber filling, whereas myocardial stiffening exacerbated diastolic dysfunction and regional mechanical heterogeneity. Secondary ionic remodelling produced marked repolarisation abnormalities but, importantly, also prolonged calcium-tension dynamics and impaired relaxation, reducing ventricular filling to an extent comparable with structural remodelling in some disease states. Increasing ionic-remodelling severity progressively amplified these effects. Despite preserved ejection fraction throughout progression, ventricular volumes decreased while global and regional myocardial deformation deteriorated. Conclusion: Diastolic dysfunction was evident before overt hypertrophy and worsened as structural, mechanical, and ionic abnormalities were added. Preserved ejection fraction did not reflect reduced ventricular filling or deterioration in myocardial strain. Regional mechanical measures may therefore reveal disease burden not captured by ejection fraction alone. By separating individual disease mechanisms, in silico modelling may help link measurable biomarkers to their underlying causes and support mechanism-based patient stratification.

papers.title: Screening Renin-Aldosterone Profiles and Long-term Cardiovascular Risk After Primary Aldosteronism Evaluation
papers.abstract: Background: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) and plasma renin activity (PRA) are measured at the screening stage of primary aldosteronism (PA) evaluation, but their prognostic relevance after confirmatory classification and subsequent treatment remains uncertain. Methods: We linked the seven-hospital Taiwan Primary Aldosteronism Investigation cohort (1991-2023) with nationwide health insurance and mortality data through June 2025. Patients were classified as confirmatory-test-defined essential hypertension (EH), PA without adrenalectomy, or PA with subsequent adrenalectomy. Covariate-adjusted Cox models evaluated screening logARR, logPRA, and logPAC separately in relation to incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure hospitalization, or cardiovascular death). Results: Among 3,178 participants (EH, 1,433; PA without adrenalectomy, 834; PA with adrenalectomy, 911), 441 (13.9%) experienced MACE during a median 7.9-year follow-up. Adjusted hazard ratios (95% CIs) per 1-unit increase in logARR were 1.09 (1.00-1.19), 1.14 (1.03-1.26), and 0.95 (0.87-1.05), respectively; corresponding logPRA estimates were 0.91 (0.83-0.99), 0.87 (0.79-0.97), and 1.04 (0.93-1.16). LogPAC showed no consistent associations. Primary biomarker-by-phenotype interactions were not significant for logARR (P=0.057) or logPRA (P=0.069); time-varying adrenalectomy analyses were supportive but exploratory. Conclusions: Higher screening ARR and lower PRA were associated with subsequent MACE in confirmatory-test-defined EH and PA without adrenalectomy, but not clearly in PA with subsequent adrenalectomy.

papers.title: Trends in Cardiovascular Risk Factors, Disease Management, and Predicted Cardiovascular Risk Among US Adults, 1999-2023
papers.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular risk factors have changed in the United States, but trends in prevalence, management, and predicted risk through the post-pandemic period remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We analyzed 11 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) periods (1999-2000 through 2021-2023) among 60,199 nonpregnant adults aged 20 years. Survey-weighted regression assessed age-standardized trends, subgroup differences, and measurement-change sensitivity. We assessed awareness, treatment, and control of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes. PREVENT equations estimated 10- and 30-year risks among adults without self-reported cardiovascular disease (CVD). Results: Obesity increased from 47.4% to 57.2% (odds ratio [OR] per decade, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.16-1.30), with class III obesity more than doubling (4.7% to 9.7%). Diabetes increased from 8.2% to 12.7% (OR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.19-1.34), while current smoking declined from 24.4% to 14.9% (OR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.71-0.81). Hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, and prior CVD showed no significant linear trends, although mean systolic blood pressure (BP) (124.2 to 120.2 mm Hg) and total cholesterol (203.6 to 188.1 mg/dL) declined, alongside improvements in other lipids. Hypertension and dyslipidemia awareness and treatment increased, but BP control peaked at 32.5% in 2013-2014 before declining to 21.5%, while LDL cholesterol control rose from 17.0% to 34.2%. Diabetes awareness increased, but treatment trends were nonsignificant. Glycemic control peaked at 51.2% in 2003-2004 before declining to 41.9% (P for nonlinearity <0.001). Predicted 10-year total CVD risk declined from 5.66% to 5.28%; atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) risk declined by 0.16 percentage points per decade (95% CI, 0.22 to 0.09), while heart failure (HF) risk increased by 0.10 (95% CI, 0.03-0.17). Their 2021-2023 estimates were nearly identical (3.20% and 3.19%, respectively); 30-year risks showed similar divergence. Conclusions: Improvements in smoking, blood pressure, and lipids coexisted with rising obesity and diabetes, declining blood pressure control after earlier gains, and divergent predicted ASCVD and HF risks.

papers.title: Near-infrared spectroscopy reveals asymmetric hemispheric blood supply during aortic arch surgery
papers.abstract: Objectives: Bilateral and trilateral selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (SACP) aim to ensure symmetric hemispheric perfusion during aortic arch surgery, which current monitoring cannot directly assess. As a step towards real-time monitoring, we assessed the feasibility of multichannel contrast-enhanced near-infrared spectroscopy (CE-NIRS) using indocyanine green and whether hemispheric bolus timing matched expectations for each perfusion configuration. Methods: In this prospective, offline-analysed pilot study, 10 patients undergoing aortic arch surgery (9 frozen elephant trunk) received 94 boluses across 10 perfusion configurations. The interhemispheric difference in time to peak ({Delta}TTP) was compared with the pre-bypass baseline using a linear mixed model with Holm correction, alongside cerebral oximetry; the relationship to postoperative cerebral injury was explored post hoc. Results: 92 of 94 boluses yielded a bilateral TTP. Contrary to expectation, the left hemisphere peaked later under bilateral (+7.2 s, 95% CI 3.4-11.0; p = 0.003) and trilateral SACP (+8.7 s, 2.5-14.8; p = 0.031). With both left-sided arch vessels on body perfusion, the asymmetry reversed (-7.0 s, -11.7 to -2.3; p = 0.025). {Delta}TTP detected 6 of 9 configuration effects, whereas oximetry detected none after correction. The three patients with cerebral injury showed the three most pronounced reversals (exact p = 0.100) but were also those managed trilaterally. Conclusions: Multichannel CE-NIRS is feasible during aortic arch surgery, without indicator-related adverse events. Bilateral and trilateral SACP did not secure symmetric indicator delivery; the configuration-dependent asymmetry and its reversal point to two steals within the perfusion circuit that oximetry missed. Their clinical relevance requires prospective confirmation.

papers.title: Provider-Level and Specialty Variation in ARNI and SGLT2i Use After Heart Failure Hospitalization
papers.abstract: BackgroundAngiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are incompletely utilized in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). The degree to which use varies at the individual level and within specialties is unknown. We aimed to characterize provider-level and specialty-level variation in ARNI and SGLT2i prescribing after HF hospitalization. MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included Veterans Affairs (VA) providers seeing patients within 6 months of HFrEF hospitalization 2017-2023. We used descriptive statistics and site-adjusted multilevel logistic regression to examine prescribing by medical specialty, provider type, and provider sex. Adjusted median odds ratios (mOR) and empirical (unadjusted) provider-level rate ratios (RRs) by percentile were used to describe provider-level variation. Clinical pharmacy visits were assessed as an independent factor and as an interaction with specialty. ResultsAmong 7,946 providers caring for 76,795 patients across 211,267 outpatient encounters, provider-level variation remained substantial after adjustment for patient characteristics and site-level clustering (mOR 1.45 for ARNI; 1.46 for SGLT2i). Within every specialty, providers ranged from near- zero to near-100% use. Relative to the median provider in the same specialty, RRs ranged from 0-0.31 (5th percentile), 0.37-0.71 (25th), 1.38-1.66 (75th), to 1.8-3.2 (95th). Cardiology visits carried the highest adjusted odds of ARNI (OR 2.30, 95% CI 2.18-2.44) and SGLT2i use (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.88-2.11) and most new starts. Pharmacist visits were independently associated with greater use of ARNI (OR 1.14, 1.06-1.23) and SGLT2i (OR 1.15, 1.06-1.24), with no effect modification by specialty. In early 2023, 58.4% (ARNI) and 40.2% (SGLT2i) of post-hospitalization HF visits had untreated patients. ConclusionsProvider-level variation in ARNI and SGLT2i use after guideline incorporation was large within every specialty and independent of site effects. Though specific specialties have higher use, individual providers, not specialty alone, may be an important target for efforts to close gaps in therapy. CLINICAL PERSPECTIVEO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIIn the years following guideline incorporation, provider-level use of ARNI and SGLT2i after heart failure hospitalization ranged from near 0% to near 100% use within every specialty. Providers at the 95th percentile prescribed at 1.8 to 3.2 times the rate the median provider of the same specialty. C_LIO_LIProvider-level variation persisted after accounting for patient characteristics and site-level clustering (median odds ratios 1.45 for ARNI and 1.46 for SGLT2i) in a health system with a national formulary and low copayments. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LIIndividual practice patterns within every specialty may be an important target for efforts to close gaps in guideline-directed therapy, and the drivers of this variation warrant study. C_LIO_LIVisits with cardiology and endocrinology providers were associated with greatest use of both medications, supporting specialty care for HF. Clinical pharmacists could play an important adjunctive role. C_LI

papers.title: Risk Factors for Progressive Cardiorenal Syndrome Events in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease: The CRIC Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is associated with poor outcomes. Risk factors for progressive CRS are not understood in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). ObjectivesThis study aimed to determine the incidence of progressive CRS and risk factors in individuals with CKD. MethodsAdults with CKD in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study excluding those with heart failure (HF) at baseline were included (n = 3,557). We defined progressive CRS as developing HF and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) within 12 months. ESKD was defined as needing renal replacement therapy or renal transplant. The associations of baseline risk factors with progressive CRS were examined using Cox proportional hazards models. A sensitivity analysis assessed risk factors in those who developed HF before ESKD and vice versa. Results161 patients (4.5%) developed progressive CRS. Traditional risk factors [multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (HR) (95% CI)] associated with progressive CRS in multivariable models included lower education [1.90 (1.28,2.83)], cardiovascular disease [1.53 (1.07,2.18)], lower estimated glomerular filtration rate [0.64 (0.51,0.82)] and higher albumin to creatinine ratio [2.44 (1.98,3.02)]. Novel risk factors associated included higher levels of alkaline phosphatase, brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-), growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), hemoglobin A1C, and lower hemoglobin. Risk factors associated with both ESKD before HF and HF before ESKD were kidney dysfunction, albuminuria, and mineral bone disorder (higher alkaline phosphatase and PTH), inflammation (TNF-), fibrotic factor (GDF-15), and anemia. Diabetes, CVD, systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, HbA1c, and BNP were more strongly associated when HF preceded ESKD. ConclusionsBoth traditional risk factors and novel risk factors associated with inflammation, mineral bone disorder, anemia, diabetes control, albuminuria, worse kidney function, and fibrotic factors are associated with progressive CRS in individuals with CKD. Many of these risk factors are modifiable representing potential areas for intervention.

papers.title: A Behaviorally Informed Patient-Facing Intervention to Promote Albuminuria Testing in Hypertension: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of KnowCKD
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlbuminuria testing to diagnose chronic kidney disease (CKD) and guide blood pressure management is recommended for adults with hypertension but remains underused in part due to suboptimal patient understanding of its importance. Patient-facing behavioral interventions have the potential to bridge this gap. We developed and evaluated KnowCKD, a behaviorally informed intervention designed to increase patient awareness of CKD and knowledge and promote albuminuria testing among adults with hypertension. MethodsKnowCKD consisted of an educational infographic and brief, behaviorally informed messages delivered to patients smartphones during the 5 days leading up to and including a scheduled primary care visit at one academic medical center. Among 57 adults with hypertension without diabetes or recent albuminuria testing, we assessed changes in CKD awareness and knowledge and patient-reported engagement via survey pre- and post-exposure to KnowCKD. Electronic Health Record (EHR)-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing was compared with 182 contemporaneous primary care controls using unmatched and propensity score-matched analysis. A post-intervention focus group evaluated participant experiences. ResultsAfter exposure to KnowCKD, recognition that adults with hypertension should undergo urine testing increased from 58% to 95%, knowledge that albuminuria indicates protein in the urine increased from 47% to 95%, and awareness that testing facilitates early CKD detection increased from 55% to 100% (P <0.001 for all). After the primary care visit, 77% of patients reported asking their clinician about urine testing and 65% reported that testing was ordered. EHR-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing occurred in 36.8% of KnowCKD participants versus 11.0% of controls (risk ratio, 3.35 [95% CI, 1.96-5.73]; absolute risk difference, 25.9 percentage points [95% CI, 12.5-39.2]). The propensity score-matched risk ratio was 2.93 (95% CI, 1.59-5.42). Participants described KnowCKD as timely, understandable, and actionable and emphasized trusted health-system communication for broader implementation. ConclusionsKnowCKD was associated with increased patient awareness of CKD and knowledge, patient engagement, and higher EHR-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing among adults with hypertension. A rigorous evaluation of KnowCKD implementation within routine health-system workflows is warranted as a next step.

papers.title: Single-cell profiling of human plaques reveals cellular and molecular signatures of symptomatic atherosclerosis
papers.abstract: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analyzed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4 T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of RGS5. Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.

papers.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Added to Statin Therapy and Cardiovascular Outcomes in ASCVD A Propensity Score-Matched Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundAdding a GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) to statin therapy in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and obesity may reduce cardiovascular risk, yet real-world evidence is limited. ObjectivesTo evaluate whether GLP-1 RA use added to statins is associated with lower all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction (MI), and ischemic stroke versus statin monotherapy in ASCVD patients with body mass index (BMI) [≥]30 kg/m2. MethodsUsing the TriNetX Research Network (108 U.S. healthcare organizations), we identified ASCVD patients with BMI [≥]30 kg/m2 on statins initiating a GLP-1 RA (n=166,278) versus statin-only controls (n=920,176). Propensity score matching on 34 covariates yielded 119,911 matched pairs followed [≤]3 years. Prespecified analyses included a BMI [≥]35 subgroup (62,385 pairs), four washout sensitivity analyses (30-120 days), and a familial hypercholesterolemia exclusion analysis (161,312 matched pairs). papers.title: Late-Stage Concentration of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Burden in US Adults: Disability-Adjusted Life Years Across AHA Stages, 2005 to 2023
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiovascular prevention is increasingly prioritised using burden estimates, yet disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) reward late-stage treatment by construction. Whether that bias is large for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, and where the population is accumulating relative to where the burden sits, is unknown. MethodsWe pooled nine National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cycles (2005-2023) and assigned CKM stages 0-4 from measured blood pressure, adiposity, glycaemia, lipids, kidney function, urine albumin, self-reported cardiovascular disease, and 10-year PREVENT risk. Years lived with disability used GBD disability weights. Years of life lost combined national death counts, stage-specific mortality from linked mortality files (1999-2018), and period life tables. A second aim attributed burden to smoking and physical inactivity, two exposures outside the CKM definition. ResultsIn 2021-2023, 13.8% of adults were stage 0, 21.3% stage 1, 49.1% stage 2, 6.5% stage 3, and 9.3% stage 4. CKM accounted for 20.0 million DALYs annually (7,881 age-standardised per 100,000), of which 4.1 million were YLD and 15.9 million attributable YLL. Stages 3-4, 15.8% of adults, generated 76% of attributable YLL; stage 4 alone generated 65% of YLD and 49% of attributable YLL. Adjusted mortality rose from stage 2 (hazard ratio 1.39) through stage 4 (3.22), while stage 1 did not differ from stage 0 (0.99; 95% CI, 0.78-1.25). Between 2006 and 2016, stage 0 prevalence fell 2.3% per year and stage 1 rose 3.1% per year. Smoking and physical inactivity accounted for 30.5% of burden (95% CI, 25.7-35.1). ConclusionsCKM burden is concentrated in stages 3-4, where excess mortality begins, while the population has been shifting into stage 1, where mortality is normal. DALY-based prioritisation will therefore systematically underfund the stage in which the next generation of patients is being created. What Is KnownO_LICKM syndrome was defined by the American Heart Association in 2023 and affects most US adults; its burden has so far been expressed only as stage prevalence. C_LIO_LIBurden estimates are used to set prevention priorities, but stage-specific health loss has not been quantified. C_LI What the Study AddsO_LICKM accounts for approximately 20.0 million DALYs per year in US adults; 76% of attributable years of life lost arise in the 15.8% of adults at stages 3-4. C_LIO_LIStage 1 carries no excess mortality after adjustment, yet has expanded by 3.1% per year since 2006, so burden and population growth sit at opposite ends of the syndrome. C_LIO_LITwo modifiable exposures outside the CKM definition, smoking and physical inactivity, account for 30.5% of burden, with inactivity contributing roughly twice as much as smoking. C_LI

papers.title: Routine CBC-Derived Markers of Systemic Inflammation Are Associated With Growth of the Dilated Ascending Aorta During CT Surveillance
papers.abstract: BackgroundAscending aortic surveillance relies on diameter thresholds, yet most dissections occur below them. Inflammation drives aortic wall remodeling independent of diameter. Inflammation drives aortic wall remodeling independent of diameter. Inflammatory indices derived from routine blood counts, such as neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), red cell distribution width (RDW), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) have been show to predict adverse cardiovascular outcomes, but their association with ascending aortic growth is unclear. Methods and ResultsWe retrospectively studied adults with [≥]2 computed tomography (CT) scans of the native ascending aorta [≥]6 months apart at a single center (2000-2023), excluding those with aortitis or no complete blood count during follow-up. Markers were summarized as 95th percentile values per patient and per scan interval. Growth was defined as a [≥]2-mm increase in mid-ascending aortic diameter. Patient-level logistic regression and interval-level generalized estimating equation models were adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, baseline diameter, systolic blood pressure, diabetes, and heritable thoracic aortic disease. Among 3,262 patients, data were available in 1,882 for RDW, 1,471 for NLR, and 1,468 for SII; 192 (10.2%) met criteria for growth. Only RDW was independently associated with growth in the overall cohort (patient level: odds ratio [OR] 1.071, 95% CI 1.002-1.144, p=0.043; interval level: OR 1.075, 95% CI 1.012-1.141, p=0.019); NLR (p=0.080) and SII (p=0.164) were not. Among patients with guideline-defined ascending aortic dilation ([≥]40 mm), all three markers were associated with interval growth (RDW OR 1.14, NLR OR 1.05, SII OR 1.01 per 100 units; all p[≤]0.014), whereas none were among aortas <40 mm; effect modification was significant for NLR (p=0.01). ConclusionsRDW was modestly associated with ascending aortic growth overall, and all three markers were associated with interval growth in patients with guideline-defined aortic dilation, suggesting that systemic inflammation may contribute to progression of aortic dilation. Prospective studies with more specific inflammatory markers are needed. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIAmong 1,882 patients undergoing serial computed tomography surveillance, higher red cell distribution width was modestly but independently associated with ascending aortic growth, whereas the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and systemic immune-inflammation index were not associated with growth in the overall cohort. C_LIO_LIIn patients with guideline-defined ascending aortic dilation ([≥]40 mm), all three inflammatory markers were associated with growth across surveillance intervals, a signal not seen in nondilated aortas. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LIRoutine blood count markers of inflammation may carry information about disease activity in patients under surveillance for ascending aortic dilation, although effect sizes are too modest for standalone risk stratification. C_LIO_LIProspective studies with standardized inflammatory panels obtained at fixed surveillance intervals are needed to test whether inflammation identifies patients with dilated aortas who are at risk of growth. papers.title: Biomarker-Informed Phenotyping of the Heart Failure Continuum: A Population-Based Evaluation of the Second Universal Definition of Heart Failure
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate a biomarker-informed, computable phenotype of the heart failure (HF) continuum, aligned with 2026 AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF Expert Consensus, using NHANES and linked mortality data, and to determine whether this phenotype identifies subgroups with distinct mortality risks. MethodsWe analyzed 11,477 U.S. adults aged [≥]20 years from the 1999-2004 NHANES cycles who participated in the surplus-sera biomarker substudy and were linked to National Death Index follow-up. Participants were classified into four phenotypes according to the 2026 Universal Definition of Heart Failure: no apparent risk, Stage A (at risk), Stage B (elevated NT-proBNP without self-reported HF), and Stage C (self-reported HF). Survey-weighted Kaplan-Meier curves and nested, multiply imputed Cox proportional hazards models, with sequential adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, and cardiometabolic covariates, were used to estimate associations with mortality. Pairwise phenotype comparisons, standardized adjusted survival estimates, and restricted mean survival times were also calculated. Incremental prognostic value was evaluated by comparing discrimination and reclassification metrics between the full phenotype and a conventional three-level model that excluded NT-proBNP. ResultsWeighted prevalences were 16.9%, 70.0%, 10.7%, and 2.4% for no apparent risk, Stage A, Stage B, and Stage C, respectively. In fully adjusted models, the hazard ratios (HRs) relative to no apparent risk were 1.58 (95% CI, 1.08-2.30), 2.88 (95% CI, 2.00-4.16), and 2.56 (95% CI, 1.61-4.09), respectively. Stage B was associated with significantly higher mortality risk than Stage A (HR, 1.83; 95% CI, 1.62-2.07), whereas the difference between Stage C and Stage B was not statistically significant (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.71-1.11). The association for Stage B attenuated less across sequentially adjusted models than that for Stage C. Adjusted 10-year mortality risks were 15.2% for Stage B and 14.2% for Stage C. Incorporating Stage B into the conventional model yielded only marginal improvements in discrimination ({Delta}C-statistic, 0.002; 95% CI, 0.001- 0.002). ConclusionA biomarker-informed phenotype of the HF continuum can be operationalized using national survey data and identifies a pre-HF subgroup with an adjusted mortality risk not significantly different from that of individuals with overt HF, despite only marginal gains in prognostic discrimination.

papers.title: Hypoxic Burden Predicts Symptomatic but Not Sleep Architecture Response to CPAP Therapy in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
papers.abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) remains the standard metric for assessing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity, although it does not fully capture the physiological consequences of respiratory events. Hypoxic burden (HB), which integrates the frequency, depth, and duration of oxygen desaturations, has been proposed as a more comprehensive measure of OSA-related hypoxic stress. This study compared the prognostic value of HB and AHI for subjective and objective treatment outcomes in patients undergoing continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy. Data from 412 patients with OSA who underwent diagnostic and CPAP-treated polysomnography were analyzed, including 52 patients with available follow-up questionnaires. HB was calculated using a validated event-based algorithm. Multivariable regression models were used to predict patient-reported outcomes and changes in sleep architecture, adjusted for age, sex and body mass index. HB consistently demonstrated stronger associations with symptomatic outcomes than AHI. Models including HB showed improved model fit and explained variance. HB remained independently associated with lower follow-up fatigue and better sleep quality after adjustment for AHI. In contrast, AHI was the dominant predictor of objective sleep architecture improvements, including increases in N3 sleep, reductions in N1 sleep, and reductions in arousal index. HB provided additional independent information only for changes in arousal burden. These findings suggest that HB and AHI capture complementary dimensions of OSA severity. While AHI primarily reflects sleep fragmentation and physiological response to CPAP, HB appears more closely related to subjective treatment benefit. Incorporating HB alongside AHI may improve clinical phenotyping and prediction of treatment response in OSA.

papers.title: Digital Twin-Based Risk Stratification Integrating Aortic Shape and Wall Mechanics in Acute Uncomplicated Type B Aortic Dissection
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThis study evaluated whether patient-specific digital twins integrating 3D aortic anatomy and structural wall stress could identify patients with acute uncomplicated type B aortic dissection (AUTBAD) at high risk for adverse aortic events. MethodsWe analyzed CTAs from 50 patients extracted from a 400 AUTBAD patient database treated with optimal medical therapy from 1999-2025. Digital twin models were constructed, and statistical shape modeling and reduced-order fluid-structure interaction analysis were performed. Anatomic shape and biomechanical stress data were integrated into models predicting freedom from aortic events, defined as intervention or aortic-related death, using leave-one-out cross-validation. A cross-validated risk score was generated for each patient, with higher scores indicating higher event risk. ResultsAt diagnosis, the median descending aortic diameter was 40.61 mm. During follow-up, 35 patients experienced an aortic event: 28 interventions (56%) and 7 aortic-related deaths (14%). Stratification by descending aortic diameter above or below 40.61 mm yielded higher-versus lower-risk aortic event-free survival of 72.0% versus 84.0% at 1 year and 27.8% versus 56.7% at 6 years (p=0.035; C-index=0.590). In the cross-validated multidimensional model combining morphology and structural stress, higher-versus lower-risk event-free survival was 60.0% versus 96.0% at 1 year and 12.5% versus 68.9% at 6 years (p View larger version (19K): org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@b59a28org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@9bcf06org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@134b721org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@1e2e788_HPS_FORMAT_FIGEXP M_FIG C_FIG Multidimensional digital twin model stratifies aortic event-free survival in AUTBAD Central MessageCombining patient-specific 3D aortic morphology and wall stress may improve identification of medically managed AUTBAD patients at high risk for aortic intervention or aortic-related death. PerspectiveTBAD geometry is highly patient specific, and one-dimensional measurements may not fully reflect patient risk. Digital twin modeling incorporating 3D morphology and wall mechanics may provide a more complete basis for risk stratification. This study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating multidimensional shape and stress data into a risk-stratification model to identify high-risk AUTBAD patients.

papers.title: Cumulative Multidomain Vulnerability and Early Mortality After Heart Transplantation: Development and Temporal Evaluation of the RIGHT-HTx Framework
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDRisk models from high-income transplant programmes may not generalise to resource-constrained settings with different recipient acuity, donor characteristics and access to mechanical circulatory support. We developed RIGHT-HTx, a parsimonious framework integrating clinical and physiological vulnerabilities, and evaluated its prognostic performance in a subsequent same-centre cohort. METHODSThis retrospective single-centre study included 436 consecutive adult heart transplant recipients (2012- 2026). Of 357 development recipients, 341 (95.5%) were score-evaluable. RIGHT-HTx incorporated three vulnerability domains: clinical acuity (INTERMACS 1-2), graded renal dysfunction (eGFR 30- 59 or 12 mmHg combined with donor-to-recipient weight ratio <1.0). A seven-point Cox-derived score underwent internal validation using 1,000 bootstrap resamples and was applied unchanged to 79 subsequent recipients. Low-, intermediate- and high-risk categories represented zero, one and [≥]2 affected domains, respectively. RESULTSAmong development recipients, 75/341 (22.0%) died within one year. Mortality increased across low-, intermediate- and high-risk categories (8.1%, 20.3% and 55.6%; log-rank P<0.001). Elevated TPG was not significantly associated with mortality individually, whereas its combination with donor undersizing was independently associated with mortality (adjusted HR 2.87, 95% CI 1.53-5.40; P=0.001). The full model improved discrimination beyond renal dysfunction alone (optimism-corrected {Delta}C-index 0.067), and the simplified score achieved an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.732. The temporal cohort more often had [≥]1 affected domain (75.9% versus 60.4%; P=0.010). Discrimination was comparable (C-index 0.738, 95% CI 0.643-0.833), although observed Kaplan- Meier one-year mortality exceeded original predictions (35.4% versus 25.4%; calibration slope 0.929). In pooled analyses (n=420), mortality increased from 8.4% (13/154) with no affected domain to 57.3% (47/82) with two or more. CONCLUSIONSRIGHT-HTx identifies cumulative multidomain vulnerability associated with early mortality after heart transplantation. Temporal discrimination was comparable, but absolute-risk calibration differed. The framework may support risk recognition and mitigation, not transplant eligibility or allocation; independent multicentre validation is required before clinical implementation.

papers.title: Early Valve Replacement vs Surveillance in Moderate Aortic Stenosis: Meta-Analysis of Randomized and Observational Evidence
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDModerate aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with excess mortality, and 2 randomized trials have tested early transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). OBJECTIVESThe authors sought to estimate the effects of early TAVR vs clinical surveillance and to compare randomized with observational estimates. METHODSSix databases and registries were searched through November 3, 2026. Adjusted observational studies were synthesized separately from trials. Certainty was rated with GRADE. RESULTSTwo trials (922 patients; TAVR UNLOAD, n = 178, HF with reduced ejection fraction; PROGRESS, n = 744, 96.4% symptomatic) and 7 cohorts were included. Early TAVR did not detectably change death over approximately 2 years (HR: 1.05; 95% CI: 0.74-1.49; low certainty), with one-fifth of the deaths needed to detect a 20% reduction. Heart failure (HF) hospitalization was lower (RR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.36-0.77; low certainty), or 70 fewer patients per 1,000 at 2 years. New pacemakers were more frequent (PROGRESS: 17.3% vs 9.3%; moderate certainty). About half of surveillance patients underwent valve replacement within 2 years. Observational cohorts estimated a 48% mortality reduction (HR: 0.52; 95% CI: 0.43-0.64; very low certainty), which differed from the randomized estimate (ratio of HRs: 2.01; 95% CI: 1.37-2.95). CONCLUSIONSIn older, predominantly symptomatic patients with moderate AS, early TAVR may make little or no difference to 2-year mortality and may reduce HF hospitalization, at the cost of more pacemakers. Because about half of patients under surveillance receive a valve within 2 years, the decision largely concerns timing. Observational survival estimates should not guide practice.

papers.title: Associations of Pathogenic Sequence Variants and Copy Number Variants with Cardiovascular and Major Clinical Outcomes in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease
papers.abstract: BackgroundGenetic abnormalities play a role in the phenotypic heterogeneity of congenital heart disease (CHD), but their associations with long-term cardiovascular outcomes in adults with congenital heart disease (ACHD) remain inadequately defined. This study examined the correlations between pathogenic sequence variations and copy number variants (CNVs) with cardiovascular and significant clinical outcomes in persons suffering from CHD. MethodsThis prospective observational cohort study included 1,000 adults with structurally confirmed CHD recruited from a tertiary care centre in Noida, India, between January 2022 and January 2026, with follow-up through August 2026. Those who have consented received exome sequencing and chromosomal microarray assessment and were categorized into four distinct, non-overlapping groups: reference, sequence-variant-only, CNV-only, and dual-positive. The primary outcome was the time to the first occurrence of any of the following events: cardiovascular death, unplanned heart failure hospitalization, resuscitated cardiac arrest, qualifying sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia, heart transplantation or durable mechanical circulatory support. Appropriate statistical analysis was performed and results were obtained. ResultsThe results showed that among the participants recruited, 800 were in the reference group, 120 had sequence variants alone, 60 had CNVs alone, and 20 had both sequence variants and CNVs. Over a median follow-up of 4.2 years, the primary outcome occurred in 12.0%, 20.0%, 25.0%, and 30.0% of participants, respectively. In the fully adjusted model, the sequence-variant-only group had an HR of 1.65 (95% CI, 1.01-2.69; nominal p = 0.0455), while the CNV-only group had an HR of 1.92 (95% CI, 1.04-3.52; nominal p = 0.0360), compared with the reference group. After Holm adjustment, neither association reached statistical significance (adjusted p = 0.072 for both comparisons). The dual-positive group had an HR of 2.12 (95% CI, 0.83-5.42; p = 0.1182). Extracardiac congenital anomalies and neurological disorders were more prevalent in those with genetic variations. Nonetheless, the secondary outcomes revealed no statistically significant correlations. ConclusionsPathogenic sequence variations and CNVs exhibited a numerically elevated adjusted risk for the primary cardiovascular composite outcome in ACHD, however neither primary association reached statistical significance after multiplicity adjustment. The findings highlight the potential significance of genetic diversity concerning clinical variability in ACHD, however they do not confirm independent prognostic significance.

papers.title: Risk-benefit assessment of oral anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation using virtual clinical trials
papers.abstract: BackgroundOral anticoagulation (OAC) reduces stroke risk in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), and screening can enable earlier AF detection and OAC initiation. However, the population-level trade-off between stroke prevention and OAC-related major bleeding for different types of AF and OAC therapy remains uncertain, and large randomized trials to resolve this are costly and time-consuming. MethodsA state-transition Markov-like model was developed to: 1) simulate the lifetime course of AF, stroke, major bleeding, and death in different virtual populations; 2) quantify benefits (stroke reduction) and harms (major bleeding) of systematic AF screening with screening-triggered OAC across CHA2DS2-VA scores; and 3) compare rhythm-guided, time-delimited ("pill-in-pocket") OAC with continuous OAC. ResultsThe model synthesized information from multiple clinical sources and reproduced stroke and bleeding incidence across clinical scenarios. At CHA2DS2-VA=2, long-term continuous rhythm monitoring (LT-CRM) with OAC lowered stroke risk (HR, 0.92 [95%CI, 0.88-0.96]) but raised bleeding risk (HR, 1.17 [95%CI, 1.07-1.27]) versus no screening. Time-to-benefit was shorter than time-to-harm for CHA2DS2-VA[≥]4, but longer for CHA2DS2-VA=0. Pill-in-pocket OAC vs continuous OAC showed no difference in stroke/mortality (HR, 1.03, 95%CI [0.91-1.16]) but lower bleeding risk (HR, 0.81, 95%CI: 0.68-0.96]) in patients with elevated bleeding risk, but not at baseline. Sensitivity analyses revealed that the risk-benefit profiles of screening or pill-in-pocket OAC strategy further depend on OAC adherence and bleeding risks. ConclusionsOur model highlights a trade-off between stroke reduction and bleeding for systematic screening-initiated OAC, with net benefit for CHA2DS2-VA[≥]4. We provide the first virtual implementation of an ongoing rhythm-guided OAC trial, showing that pill-in-pocket OAC may lower bleeding risk compared to continuous OAC, highlighting the potential of virtual clinical trials to guide clinical trial design.

papers.title: Uncovering Distinct Phenotypes of Early Onset Heart Failure in Women
papers.abstract: BackgroundHeart failure in younger women is understudied and may reflect heterogeneous pathways and risk not adequately captured by conventional classifications. We aimed to identify clinically distinct phenotypes of early-onset heart failure in women, assess their prognostic significance, and evaluate their transportability in an independent national cohort. MethodsWe identified women aged 18-55 years with heart failure using electronic health record data from a large multi-hospital system. A variational deep embedding model incorporating 283 clinical features was used for unsupervised phenotyping. Associations with subsequent inpatient hospitalization, emergency department utilization, and mortality were evaluated using age-stratified Cox models. Phenotype transportability was assessed by both applying the institutionally trained model and by independent de novo clustering as a replication analysis in the All of Us cohort. ResultsAmong 1,407 young women with heart failure (median age, 45 years), four phenotypes were identified: hypertensive pregnancy (n=494), cardiorenal (n=276), autoimmune (n=394), and cardiometabolic-ischemic (n=243), with a bootstrap adjusted Rand index of 0.65 and silhouette score of 0.45. Compared with the hypertensive pregnancy phenotype, risks of inpatient hospitalization were highest for the cardiorenal (HR 2.86 [95% CI, 2.35-3.49]) and autoimmune (HR 2.25 [95% CI, 1.87-2.70]) phenotypes; mortality risks were similarly elevated (HR 4.65 [95% CI, 3.17-6.82] and HR 4.38 [95% CI, 3.03-6.31], respectively) in these two groups. In All of Us participants (n=682), transferred phenotypes retained their principal clinical characteristics and continued to stratify hospitalization risk. Independent clustering most strongly reproduced the cardiorenal phenotype (Jaccard index, 0.744). ConclusionsEarly-onset heart failure in women comprises distinct cardio-obstetric, cardiorenal, autoimmune, and cardiometabolic-ischemic phenotypes with divergent clinical outcomes. These findings support a life-course approach to heart failure classification in women that complements conventional frameworks and incorporates pregnancy history and female-predominant systemic conditions. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSUnsupervised machine learning identifies distinct clinical phenotypes of heart failure among young women, highlighting heterogeneity in a population that remains understudied. These phenotypes captured differing cardiometabolic, cardiovascular, and pregnancy-related characteristics, suggesting potentially distinct pathways contributing to heart failure development. External validation in the All of Us cohort supported external validity and demonstrated the potential for identifying these patterns across diverse healthcare populations. What Are the Clinical Implications?Heart failure in young women is clinically diverse, underscoring the importance of comprehensive assessment beyond traditional heart failure classifications, including cardiometabolic risk factors and pregnancy history. Recognition of distinct clinical phenotypes may help clinicians identify women with differing risk profiles and inform more individualized approaches to cardiovascular evaluation, risk factor management, and longitudinal follow-up. Further studies are needed to determine whether phenotypes differ in treatment responses and whether phenotype-guided management can improve outcomes.

papers.title: Waist-to-Height Ratio Identifies Cardiometabolic Risk Not Captured by Body Mass Index: The All of Us Research Program
papers.abstract: BackgroundBody mass index (BMI) does not characterize central adiposity and may obscure cardiometabolic risk among adults classified as normal weight. We evaluated associations between waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) and incident disease across the BMI spectrum and among adults with normal BMI. MethodsWe studied 308,600 adults in the All of Us Research Program. Participants with the corresponding prevalent disease were excluded separately for eight cardiometabolic outcomes. Cause-specific Cox models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, smoking, and BMI-related factors. We evaluated continuous and nonlinear WHtR associations, elevated WHtR among normal-BMI adults, and incremental discrimination. Additional analyses tested WHtR-by-BMI-category interactions. ResultsAmong 77,684 adults with normal BMI, 24,301 (31.3%) had WHtR [≥]0.50. In whole-cohort analyses, adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) per 0.05 higher WHtR ranged from 1.07 to 1.31 across the eight outcomes. In BMI-stratified interaction models, corresponding diabetes HRs were 1.52 (95% CI, 1.43-1.61) in normal BMI, 1.42 (1.36-1.49) in overweight, and 1.22 (1.20-1.25) in obesity (P for interaction <0.001). Hypertension associations also differed across BMI groups (P for interaction <0.001). Among normal-BMI adults, WHtR [≥]0.50 versus <0.50 was associated with diabetes (HR, 1.74), myocardial infarction (1.49), and ischemic stroke (1.52). Associations with all eight outcomes persisted in normal-BMI landmark analyses excluding the first year. Flexible age adjustment preserved the principal findings. Adding nonlinear WHtR improved cross-validated discrimination, most notably for diabetes ({Delta}C-index=0.0134). ConclusionsWHtR identified cardiometabolic risk beyond BMI classification. Associations with diabetes and hypertension were particularly pronounced among normal-BMI adults, supporting assessment of central adiposity alongside BMI. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIIn this longitudinal cohort of 308,600 adults, higher waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) was associated with incident type 2 diabetes, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and chronic kidney disease independently of body mass index (BMI). C_LIO_LIAmong adults with normal BMI, 31.3% had WHtR [≥]0.50, identifying a phenotype associated with higher incidence of all eight evaluated cardiometabolic outcomes. These associations persisted after excluding the first year of follow-up. C_LIO_LIThe association between continuous WHtR and incident diabetes was stronger among adults with normal BMI than among those with obesity. For hypertension, the association was stronger in normal-BMI adults than in both overweight and obesity. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LIBMI alone can miss clinically relevant central adiposity and associated cardiometabolic risk among adults classified as having normal weight. C_LIO_LIWHtR is a practical complementary measure that clinicians may consider alongside BMI during preventive cardiometabolic assessment, particularly when a patient has a normal BMI but other risk factors or clinical concerns. C_LIO_LIWHtR should not be treated as a stand-alone risk model or a universal treatment threshold; its incremental prognostic value and exposure-response patterns differed by outcome. C_LI

papers.title: Overall Outlook on Life and Cardiovascular Health Behaviors among Adolescent and Young Adult Females: A Cross-sectional Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among women, with risk factors commonly emerging during adolescence. Emerging evidence indicates that psychological factors, such as optimism, affect cardiovascular health, yet this remains understudied among young women. To assess the association between overall outlook on life and preventive cardiovascular health behaviors among young women. MethodsWe conducted a secondary analysis of a cohort of 331 young women aged 15 to 24 years who completed the modified American Heart Association Womens Health Survey (2017-2018), using multivariate regression adjusted for confounding. ResultsOver 50% of young women felt their outlook on life may impact their likelihood of developing a serious illness such as heart disease. Outlook on life was associated with prioritizing and taking care of health ({beta}=0.18-0.19, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) [0.09, 0.29]; P=0.002) and usually following recommended healthy eating ({beta}=0.12, 95% CI [0.03, 0.23]; P=0.016). Young women who identified as black (27.5%; N=91) felt that their outlook on life had a lower impact on their likelihood of developing a serious illness such as heart disease (Odds Ratio (OR)=0.80; 95% CI [0.65, 0.98]; P = 0.04), compared to other racial groups. ConclusionOur findings support previous observations indicating a cardioprotective role of optimism in cardiovascular health. However, this association may not hold among young women of color, potentially reflecting constraints in their lived environment that limit how much a positive outlook translates into perceived control over health outcomes. Strategies to reduce cardiovascular disease in women should address young womens cardiovascular health and psychological and contextual factors, with particular attention to young women of color.

papers.title: Door-to-Valve Time and Clinical Outcomes in Acute Decompensated Severe Aortic Stenosis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundAcute decompensated aortic stenosis (ADAS) carries high mortality, but the optimal timing of valve intervention is unknown. ObjectiveTo assess the association between time to valve intervention (transcatheter aortic valve replacement [TAVR] or balloon aortic valvuloplasty [BAV]) and clinical outcomes in ADAS. MethodsEmbase, Ovid MEDLINE and CENTRAL were searched to May 15, 2026. Hazard ratios (HRs) for delayed versus earlier intervention were pooled using random-effects models with modified Hartung-Knapp inference. Unadjusted short-term mortality risk ratios (RRs) were pooled using the Mantel-Haenszel method. ResultsEight observational cohort studies (n=6,044) met inclusion criteria: six TAVR (n= 5,986) and two BAV (n=58) studies. Patients were approximately 79 years old, and 63% were male. Early-intervention thresholds ranged from <24-48 hours (BAV) to [≤]22 days (TAVR) from admission. Delayed intervention was not significantly associated with long-term all-cause mortality (HR 1.52, 95% CI 0.46-5.00; p=0.269; I2=58.2%) or mortality per five-day delay (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.34-3.43; p=0.530; I2=86.7%). Crude short-term mortality was higher with delayed intervention (RR 4.96, 95% CI 1.17-20.92; p=0.029; I2=0.0%), although this association was not robust to sensitivity analyses. Most studies were at serious risk of bias, with substantial heterogeneity in clinical severity, intervention timing, and treatment modality. ConclusionPoint estimates favour earlier intervention, but current observational data do not establish a mortality benefit for an optimal door-to-valve interval, and existing study designs are biased against early treatment. Prospective and randomized-controlled trials on optimal valve intervention timing following ADAS are needed.

papers.title: Trajectories of Estimated Glucose Disposal Rate and Risk of Cardiovascular Disease: Evidence from Two Prospective Cohorts
papers.abstract: BackgroundEstimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR) is an accessible surrogate of insulin sensitivity and has been associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. However, whether longitudinal eGDR trajectory patterns convey prognostic information beyond cumulative eGDR exposure remains unclear. We aimed to characterize distinct eGDR trajectories and evaluate their associations with incident CVD in two prospective cohorts. MethodsWe included 4,823 CVD-free adults aged 45 years or older from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS, n=3,258) and the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA, n=1,565). Latent class mixed models identified four eGDR trajectory classes across three waves. Associations with incident CVD were examined using multivariable Cox models. We further fitted joint models including both trajectory class and cumulative average eGDR to assess their independent contributions. ResultsCompared with the persistently high trajectory, the persistently low and declining trajectories were associated with higher CVD risk in both cohorts. In joint models, whereas trajectory class showed residual prognostic signal, particularly in HRS, with directionally consistent but less precise estimates in ELSA. In HRS, adding trajectory class improved model fit beyond cumulative average eGDR alone, whereas adding cumulative average eGDR to the trajectory model did not. Direct pairwise comparisons showed that the declining-then-rising trajectory was associated with lower risk than the declining trajectory in HRS, with directionally similar but imprecise estimates in ELSA. ConclusionsLongitudinal eGDR trajectory patterns may convey prognostic information not fully captured by cumulative average eGDR alone. These findings suggest that the temporal pattern of insulin sensitivity may be clinically relevant in addition to cumulative exposure, while the potentially favorable profile of recovery trajectories warrants cautious interpretation and external replication. papers.title: Interpretable ECG manifolds link longitudinal electrical phenotypes to heart-failure risk in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
papers.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) produces heterogeneous electrical phenotypes whose continuous organization, longitudinal evolution and clinical relevance remain poorly defined. We developed complementary variational-autoencoder representations to map HCM ECG morphology relative to physiological variation and characterize within-subject change. Using 5,194 normal-reference ECGs and 2,594 longitudinal visits from 650 individuals with HCM, we found that HCM overlapped the physiological manifold but extended towards its periphery, while an HCM-oriented manifold largely reorganized shared electrical modes. Mixed-effects models identified longitudinal drift in selected phenotypic axes. A lateral/frontal QRS-force coordinate remained time-dependent after censoring septal reduction therapy, atrial fibrillation and pacing, and lower values were associated with subsequent heart-failure risk in baseline and time-updated analyses. A time-conditioned change VAE identified four interpretable within-subject modes aligned with longer-term trajectories. Sarcomeric genotype was associated with phenotype position but not trajectory rate.

papers.title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in diabetic patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction - real world outcomes
papers.abstract: AimsTo evaluate the effectiveness of GLP-1 RAs on clinical outcomes in diabetic patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Methods and resultsIn this retrospective observational cohort study, all adults with diabetes mellitus and HFrEF between 2014 and 2025 were identified. Patients treated with GLP-1 RAs were matched to controls using stratified exact matching. The primary outcome was a composite of heart failure hospitalization or all-cause mortality. Treatment effects were estimated using nonparametric bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations) to derive risk ratios, NNT estimates, and corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Time-to-event analyses using Cox proportional hazards models were performed as a validation analysis. Among 7,878 patients with HFrEF, 793 (10.1%) patients who initiated GLP-1 RA therapy after HF diagnosis were matched to 1,825 controls. GLP-1 receptor agonist use was associated with a lower risk of heart failure hospitalization or death, with risk ratios of 0.58 (95% CI: 0.42-0.77) at 12 months and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.61-0.85) at 36 months. The combination of high baseline event rates and substantial relative risk reduction translated into remarkably low NNT values in the overall population, with an NNT of 17 (95% CI: 11-33) at 1 year and 13 (95% CI: 8-25) at 3 years. Post hoc subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent effects across clinical subgroups, with no significant heterogeneity observed. ConclusionIn this large real-world cohort of diabetic patients with HFrEF, GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy, in addition to guideline-directed medical therapy, was associated with a lower risk of death or heart failure hospitalization.
